articles.title: The Full 12 Rounds
articles.description: Adam Wagner’s Sunday puzzle will get solvers coming and going.
articles.content:
SUNDAY PUZZLE — Will Shortz, in his print introduction to this grid, writes: “Adam Wagner, of Oakland, Calif., is a creative lead at Patreon, a monetization platform for content creators. He’s the creator of the online games Shuffalo and Catalogues on The New Yorker’s website. Adam says it’s ‘crossword kismet’ that the six theme examples in this puzzle worked out perfectly in length, interlock and symmetry. Sometimes a crossword is just meant to be.”
Talk about a lot of moving parts! This puzzle was a doozy for me to make sense of, but once everything clicks into place, it’s a beautifully elegant system.
Today’s Theme
Solvers will notice six rectangular arrangements of gray boxes in this grid. They are all two squares tall and six squares wide, and each has a black outline with rounded corners and four arrows that indicate clockwise or counterclockwise movement. Each rectangle also has a thick vertical line separating two squares in its top or bottom row. There are also two extremely helpful revealer entries, at 49- and 85-Across, the first of which illuminates a high-end feature of these shapes that I didn’t recognize on my own.
The way the clues work in this theme set is confusing before you get a handle on the trick. There are six clues that stand out because they make no sense, on first glance, and they also run through six of the 12 rows that make up the gray rectangles. These appear at 19-, 28-, 66-, 73-, 112- and 124-Across — all of the gray rows with those thick lines, which turns out to be relevant — and all are jumbles of words and punctuation. 19A, for example, is [ … in global commerce)(Conflict … ].
The rectangles contain six more rows, above or below the ones already mentioned. Two of them are stand-alone entries with their own clues: 22A, [Potential benefit], which runs below 19A and forms the topmost rectangle, and 121A, [Certain factory machine], which is paired with 124A at the bottom of the grid. The remaining four are six-letter runs in longer entries; you’ll see those in 32-, 68-, 70- and 103-Across.
The shape at 19- and 22-Across is a good gateway to unraveling this confounding mechanism. This is where I cracked the code (i.e., used the brute force of letters from crossing entries to fill in every square). 1-Down, [Bewilder], is a hilariously apt clue for this spot in the puzzle: It solves to STUMP, which means that T is the first letter in 19A, and U is the first letter of 22A. With the additional help of 2- through 6-Down, which are reasonably easy to deduce for Sunday solvers, I had every letter in each entry. 19A is TETRAD, and 22A is UPSIDE, which goes with the clue [Potential benefit].

articles.title: Lamborghini focused on hybrid future, not manual transmissions
articles.description: The famed Italian performance car brand admits some customers still want a manual, but says its priority is evolving its new hybrid supercar formula.
articles.content:
Lamborghini won't follow Ferrari in bringing back the manual transmission, with its focus instead firmly on further developing its new generation of hybrid supercars.
"I think there will always be Lamborghini customers asking for a manual transmission, and for everything that is rooted in our tradition," Temerario product line director Paolo Racchetti told CarExpert in Milan, Italy.
"But on the other hand, Lamborghini is defined by always evolving and thinking about the future. We are the most innovative brand in the super-sports car segment, and at this moment our target is to evolve this new architecture even further.
"It is already delivering a lot of performance and a lot of emotion, and we really think we can enhance both even further.
"So, for the moment, we will keep moving in this direction and continue with the product philosophy defined by our Cor Tauri [bull's heart] strategy."
First outlined in 2021, Direzione Cor Tauri is Lamborghini's strategic roadmap for electrifying its product range and decarbonising its operations.
As it stands, the Italian exotic automaker aims to reduce enterprise emissions by 40 per cent per car by 2030.
On the product side, Lamborghini has so far introduced two plug-in hybrid (PHEV) supercars – the Revuelto and Temerario – while also transitioning its SUV, the Urus, to PHEV power.
The roadmap makes no mention of manual transmissions, which have been absent from the Lamborghini lineup since the Gallardo ended production more than a decade ago.
Mr Racchetti's comments suggest there are currently no plans to reintroduce three pedals and a stick shift in future models.
Conversely, Ferrari is chasing the favour of traditionalists with the new 12Cilindri Manuale – its first factory-built manual model since the California.
That said, the gearbox in question isn't a true manual in the traditional sense. Rather than engineering a new H-pattern transmission, Ferrari has created what it calls a 'Manuale By-Wire' system, combining a traditional-looking gated gear shifter and clutch pedal with the company's existing eight-speed dual-clutch automatic transmission.
McLaren, meanwhile, is set to revive the manual with the McL 6GT, an ultra-exclusive production supercar due to enter production in 2028 – more than three decades after the legendary F1 became the brand's last manual road car.
Indeed, manual transmissions have become increasingly rare among modern supercars, often reserved for limited-run models or special projects.

Qualcomm (QCOM) Unveils Auto And Edge AI Push At Snapdragon Summit
September 26, 2026
SI
Reviewed by Bailey
QUALCOMM (NasdaqGS:QCOM) used its latest Snapdragon Summit to spotlight new automotive and edge AI capabilities built around the Snapdragon Digital Chassis platform.
Management outlined deeper integration of agentic AI in vehicles and edge devices, positioning Snapdragon as a core compute layer for connected products.
The firm highlighted expanded Snapdragon use in Microsoft Surface devices and branded partnerships with Manchester United and the Mercedes F1 team.
These Snapdragon Digital Chassis and Surface partnership updates matter, but they are only one piece of the Qualcomm investment puzzle. Our analysis turns up for QUALCOMM as well.
Qualcomm is not the only business tied to the build out of AI and connected hardware, so it is worth comparing it with peers exposed to .
QUALCOMM develops and licenses wireless technologies that sit inside smartphones and a growing range of connected hardware, so its push into the Digital Chassis and edge AI tools ties its chip designs and software stacks more tightly to automakers and device makers across the industry.
Advertisement
Qualcomm’s Snapdragon partnerships test the “non‑handset QCT” bet
The Qualcomm Narrative rests on one big idea. The handset cash engine has to fund AI-heavy platforms in autos, PCs, IoT and data centers so that non-handset QCT revenue grows into a meaningful counterweight.
"The main thing that has to go right is execution on large new AI and compute programs in data center, automotive and industrial IoT so that these businesses offset pressure from smartphone cyclicality, higher wafer costs and the loss of Apple modem revenue..."
See how the full story points towards .
The Digital Chassis push, deeper agentic AI in cars and expanded Microsoft Surface wins all speak directly to that non-handset ramp the Narrative leans on. These deals give Qualcomm a clearer route to put Snapdragon into vehicles and Windows laptops where Nvidia and AMD are also targeting AI workloads. This supports the idea of a broader compute footprint rather than a handset-only story.
There is a flip side. Automotive and edge AI are now even more central to justifying the guided US$40b non-handset QCT goal, so any slowdown in design wins or weaker attach rates would cut into the very offset to smartphone and Apple modem risk analysts are counting on. The balance tilts modestly to the bull case here, but only if you already buy into that execution-heavy Narrative.
Ultimately these Snapdragon partnerships only matter to you in so far as they either reinforce or weaken the investment story you already believe about Qualcomm’s shift away from handset dependence.
